extracted.intended_audience: FCC program administrators, SDOs, regulated entities and their counsel, compliance officers, and commenters on suspension/debarment rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and supplemental rules governing suspension, debarment, limited denial of participation (LDP), evidentiary presentation, imputation of conduct, appeals, covered transactions, and participant tiering for FCC non-procurement programs (notably USF, TRS, and NDBEDP).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-notice letters policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-notice letters may be a useful tool in appropriate circumstances (for example, if misconduct should be resolved through an administrative agreement), but the issuance of pre-notice letters will not be mandatory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not require pre-notice letters in all cases; agencies have not made them mandatory historically and requiring them could impede rapid action to protect programs and beneficiaries. Use pre-notice letters 'whenever possible' where beneficial, but reserve agency flexibility to move quickly when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imputation of conduct (general rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Guidelines' imputation rule permits the agency to impute conduct from an individual to an organization, from an organization to an individual, among individuals, or among organizations in appropriate circumstances; the rule is permissive (the agency 'may' impute) and affords flexibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SDOs should consider individual facts case-by-case. Imputation is not mandatory and may be applied where necessary to protect programs and beneficiaries; potential harm to 'good actors' within an organization does not preclude imputation where overall harm to programs outweighs that concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imputation factors and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: While imputation from an individual to an organization will often be most appropriate based on the organization's knowledge, approval, or acquiescence, imputation may also be appropriate because of inadequate supervision or oversight; imputation need not be limited to conduct within the scope of employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject limiting imputation to acts 'within the scope of employment' as it could miss scenarios where an organization knew of or benefited from misconduct outside formal scope. Providers may present evidence to demonstrate why the SDO should not impute liability in particular situations (e.g., good-faith efforts to identify third-party actions). Section 180.630 permits (but does not require) imputation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation of evidence responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the Office of Inspector General (OIG) conducted the underlying investigation supporting suspension/debarment, the OIG should generally have primary responsibility for providing information to the SDO; in other situations, appropriate Commission units (e.g., Enforcement Bureau) may present with input from program bureaus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SDO may designate a Commission unit primarily responsible for sharing relevant materials to inform decisionmaking and should establish coordination procedures for other bureaus/offices when necessary. Proceedings are to be 'informal' and reflect the SDO's managerial decision functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconsideration and Commission review — initial vs final suspension decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: An initial suspension decision (the date the SDO first signs a suspension order) is interlocutory and not subject to petition for reconsideration (PFR) or AFR; a final suspension decision (issued after opportunity to respond and an informal proceeding, with written findings of fact) may be the subject of reconsideration or Commission review where otherwise permitted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties may not file PFR or AFR of initial suspension decisions because they are interlocutory and do not consummate decisionmaking. Reconsideration of final suspension decisions is expressly permitted under section 1.106. If a party does not oppose the initial suspension, it waives the right to challenge the final suspension decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timelines for reconsideration and review
rubrics_metrics.description: Reconsideration and Commission review of suspension decisions should be subject to reasonable timelines: SDOs must resolve any PFR of a final suspension decision within 45 days (may extend for good cause); the Commission should endeavor to resolve AFRs of final suspension decisions within 180 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject a 90-day constructive denial rule as inconsistent with Guidelines. These timelines aim to prevent unduly lengthy proceedings; extensions allowed for good cause at SDO discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stay standard for final suspension/debarment orders
rubrics_metrics.description: A final suspension decision is a non-hearing order resolving an informal proceeding and is subject to a permissive stay under §1.102(b); stay requests will be evaluated under the four Virginia Petroleum Jobbers criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The four criteria: (1) likelihood of success on the merits; (2) irreparable injury without a stay; (3) degree of injury to other parties if relief is granted; (4) whether a stay is in the public interest. Do not adopt automatic stays (e.g., for failure to rule within a timeframe) nor automatic stays upon filing an AFR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Debarment reconsideration/review/appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Reconsideration, review, and appeal of debarment decisions generally follow the same rules and standards as for suspensions; debarments become effective after the SDO issues a final debarment order and may be subject to AFR under §1.115.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Debarments are non-hearing orders subject to permissive stay under §1.102(b). The Guidelines' reconsideration rule for debarments is adopted, and standard appeal/review mechanisms apply as with suspensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adoption of Limited Denial of Participation (LDP) remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission adopts an LDP mechanism as a flexible remedy to supplement suspensions and debarments; an LDP prevents participation in particular FCC programs or geographic regions but does not trigger governmentwide reciprocity (no SAM.gov effect).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An LDP requires notice and opportunity to be heard before issuance. LDPs provide additional due process protections and investigative flexibility, and the Commission remains free to use other investigative tools or subsequently initiate suspension/debarment if warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability and scope of LDPs
rubrics_metrics.description: LDPs are available only for misconduct arising from agency programs subject to the Commission's suspension or debarment rules; the SDO may extend an LDP beyond the program where misconduct occurred to other Commission programs subject to LDPs depending on facts and circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not broaden LDPs to programs outside the current scope. When extending an LDP, the SDO should consider service disruptions and customer impacts and provide for transitions or continuations of services to mitigate harm, similar to suspension/debarment remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: LDP causes and factors
rubrics_metrics.description: In evaluating whether to issue an LDP, the SDO should consider the totality of the circumstances, the factors in section 180.860 of the Guidelines, and additional factors such as whether the misconduct was isolated, how egregious it was, and whether the violator promptly and fully self-reported or took concrete steps to come into compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If alleged misconduct involves causes set forth in section 180.800(a) of the Guidelines, or a criminal indictment/conviction or evidence of fraud, the presumption is that suspension is the more appropriate remedy. 'Unsatisfactory risk' is not impermissibly vague and is consistent with governmentwide guidance on program risk management.

rubrics_metrics.name: LDP evidentiary standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission adopts an 'adequate evidence' evidentiary standard for LDPs, consistent with the evidentiary standard for suspension under the Guidelines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two per se circumstances constitute adequate evidence: (1) an existing LDP related to any Commission program may constitute adequate evidence to enter a concurrent LDP for other programs; (2) filing of a criminal indictment or information (regardless of whether based on offenses against or related to the Commission) constitutes adequate evidence for LDP actions. Other circumstances may also meet 'adequate evidence.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Initiating an LDP proceeding
rubrics_metrics.description: An LDP proceeding may be initiated by the head of any bureau or office that determines an LDP would be appropriate (based on causes/factors) by referring the matter to the SDO with supporting documentation; the SDO, after consultation, determines whether to proceed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the SDO determines an LDP is appropriate, it must promptly provide notice specifying causes for the proposed LDP, potential effects (including possible length and affected FCC programs/geographic areas), and the recipient's rights to contest (seek a conference, provide documents, or both). The notice must state that the person has 15 days to respond. An LDP may be initiated during a suspension/debarment proceeding, suspending that proceeding and incorporating the record into the LDP record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative agreements and compliance agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative agreements, including compliance agreements, may supplement an LDP or serve as an alternative to an LDP to allow maximum flexibility in fashioning a remedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative remedies may be implemented only after consultation with the bureaus/offices responsible for the programs in which misconduct occurred, and compliance agreements require consultation with and approval by OGC.

rubrics_metrics.name: LDP period and extension criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The SDO may impose an LDP for any term up to 12 months and may grant one extension of up to six additional months (not to exceed 18 months total).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensions should be imposed if review during the initial period: (i) fails to show full compliance with LDP terms or supplemental agreements; or (ii) shows other misconduct in Commission programs subject to the remedy or new causes sufficient to support extension. During initial or extended LDP periods, the SDO may initiate a suspension/debarment proceeding if warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: SDO authority to conduct LDP proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: Authority to conduct LDP proceedings is consolidated under the SDO rather than residing with bureaus administering relevant programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consolidation is intended to streamline administration, promote consistency, and facilitate conversion between LDP and exclusion proceedings where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Converting LDP proceedings to suspension/debarment proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: If after initiation of an LDP the SDO learns of new facts showing more serious misconduct, the SDO may initiate an exclusion (suspension/debarment) proceeding after consulting with relevant bureaus; LDP proceedings are stayed for 30 days to allow respondents to contest a proposed suspension/debarment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the respondent contests the proposed exclusion, proceedings are consolidated and the LDP record is incorporated into the exclusion proceeding. If a subject of an LDP fails to comply with its terms, the SDO may initiate an exclusion proceeding; where both are pending, the LDP remains operative while the exclusion is contested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imputation of conduct in LDP proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission may impute conduct in LDP proceedings in the same manner as provided under section 180.630 of the Guidelines for exclusion proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the same permissive imputation framework and case-by-case considerations in LDP contexts as for suspensions/debarments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and scope of 'covered transactions'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Guidelines define 'non-procurement transactions' broadly as any transaction (except procurement contracts) including grants, cooperative agreements, scholarships, fellowships, contracts of assistance, loans, loan guarantees, subsidies, insurances, payments for specified uses, and donation agreements; agencies have flexibility to determine which nonprocurement transactions are covered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procurement contracts awarded directly by a federal agency are not covered; however, contracts awarded by non-federal participants are covered if the contract amount equals or exceeds $25,000. Agencies may tailor coverage consistent with governmentwide guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Covered Programs included/excluded by Commission
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission applies the modified Guidelines and supplemental rules to nonprocurement transactions under the USF programs, TRS programs, and the NDBEDP; other Commission transactions (e.g., section 214 authorizations, equipment authorizations, broadcast and spectrum licenses, incentive auction/repacking payments) are excluded at this time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decision to include these Covered Programs is based on program disbursements and audit/IG reports indicating the need for stronger oversight. Excluded programs may remain governed by separate Commission remedies; the rules do not extend to transactions to/from licensees and those with spectrum usage rights, except where such entities participate in the Covered Programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participant tiers (primary and lower tier) and lower-tier criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: The Guidelines use 'tiers' (primary and lower) to categorize participants; primary tier participants deal directly with the agency/program administrators; lower tier participants deal with persons at the next higher tier. The adopted lower tier definition includes contractors, subcontractors, suppliers, consultants, or their agents/representatives if they also satisfy at least one of: (1) material role relating to or significantly affecting claims for disbursements; (2) are considered a 'principal'; or (3) the transaction amount is expected to be at least $25,000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies have discretion to designate participants as primary, lower, or neither. Expanding lower tier designations (including subcontractors and suppliers) enhances oversight without imposing onerous requirements. Lower tier participants are subject to required disclosures and may be subject to exclusion when justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision against broadening covered programs now
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules will not extend at this time to transactions under the Commission's other currently existing programs nor to transactions to/from licensees and those with spectrum usage rights (except for Covered Programs' participation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach reflects record support and recognizes that other transactions are governed by separate Commission rules; interested parties may raise scope concerns in other proceedings or petitions for rulemaking.
